items.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000
items.q: And Alvin Batiste is one of those people who hears a certain way.

ctx.x: I have to say listening to one particular solo you played today, that you really have what I consider to be a composer’s sense in your improvising. There’s a great use of a mixture of chording, rhythmic things, and you did something just in octaves, you know, one octave delayed off the other, and I mean it’s a great device.

I try to use material that sort of either — I can’t say needs development — but develops itself. I try to let the music develop itself. That’s what I try to do. When I make a conscious effort at it it doesn’t work. But when I make a feeling effort, in other words when I let the music flow out, then it works. And whatever I have to do to get it out, it’s not so much that I’m forcing the physical part, the physical part happens. Like sometimes I can hear repeated notes. Fortunately for me I had teachers who taught…
Well somebody called it, jazz was the music of surprise, so I guess — mostly good surprises.
